To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the discursive strategies of wildlife and recreational organisations were instrumental in redefining the Quebec forest regime.
wildlife and recreational organisations have successfully used discursive strategies to redefine the forest regime in Quebec.

the discursive strategies of the stakeholders in the case of the Commission on the Sustainability of Public Forest Management in Quebec are based on the economic discourse, and the alliance of wildlife stakeholders with environmental groups is the result of their strategic use of economic discourse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How did wildlife organisations use discursive strategies to gain recognition?
the discursive strategies of social actors and their effects on the definition of a public policy.
the way social actors use discursive strategies in order to influence decision-making processes and the redefinition, through public participation, of the forestry regime in Quebec.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the economic discourse remains dominant, but the arguments most likely taken into account are the ones which combine environmental and economic concerns.

the economic discourse has been the most influential in the redefinition of the forest regime, but that the environmental discourse, which has been used in a strategic manner, is gaining in influence and will probably become the most influential in future forest management.
the economic discourse remains hegemonic and that the environmental and social discourses are still marginalised, but that the environmental discourse is more likely to be heard than the social one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the discursive strategies of social actors have been successful in changing the way the forest regime is defined in Quebec.
the economic discourse is the most powerful, and that environmental groups have to use economic arguments to gain legitimacy.
we need to pay more attention to the role of discourses in shaping the political process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
public participation processes are not neutral, but rather a tool for social actors to gain legitimacy and influence policy-making processes.
the discursive strategies of social actors can influence the way in which public policies are designed.
social and economic arguments are not necessarily incompatible and that a coalition can be formed to promote a new vision of forest governance.
